title: Prices that do not crash
brief: Our supplier sends a price list every week and someone always types n/a or a comma instead of a dot. My little script crashes on the first bad line and I get nothing. I want the total of the good prices and a note for each bad one.

skill.title: try / except catches the errors you expect
skill.card: float("n/a") raises a ValueError and stops the program. Put the risky line in a try: block and handle the problem in except ValueError:, and the loop goes on with the next line. Catch the specific error, never a bare except:.

task: The first input line is the number of lines that follow. Each of those lines is name;price. For each price that float() cannot read, print Bad price: and the name. At the end print the total of the good prices with 2 decimals: ~~~text Bad price: paper A4 Bad price: pens x10 Total: 66.00 ~~~
starter:
n = int(input())
total = 0
for _ in range(n):
    name, price = input().split(";")
    total += float(price)
print(f"Total: {total:.2f}")
hint: Wrap total += float(price) in try:, and print the Bad price line in except ValueError:.

pens x10;3,50

title: A picking list for the warehouse
brief: The shop drops an orders.txt file in our folder every morning. My pickers want a picking.txt they can print, with a box to tick on each line. Blank lines in the order file are just noise.

skill.title: open() with with
skill.card: with open("name.txt") as f: opens a file and closes it for you at the end of the block. Loop on f to get one line at a time (with its \n, so strip() it). Open with "w" to write, and add \n yourself at the end of each line.
skill.example:
with open("demo.txt", "w") as out:
    out.write("first\n")
    out.write("second\n")
with open("demo.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print("Read:", line.strip())

task: Read orders.txt: each non empty line is SKU;quantity. Write picking.txt with one line per order, like [ ] 3 x A-100, in the same order. Then print the number of lines written: ~~~text Picking list: 4 lines ~~~
solution:
with open("orders.txt") as f:
    lines = [line.strip() for line in f if line.strip()]
with open("picking.txt", "w") as out:
    for line in lines:
        sku, qty = line.split(";")
        out.write(f"[ ] {qty} x {sku}\n")
print(f"Picking list: {len(lines)} lines")
hint: Keep only the stripped lines that are not empty, then split each one on ";" and write f"[ ] {qty} x {sku}\n".

tests.output: Picking list: 4 lines

got = _fs["picking.txt"].splitlines()

" + "

title: Which invoices are late?
brief: Our clients pay at 30 days. Every morning I scroll through the invoice list and count days on my fingers. Give me the late ones and how late they are, please. I will type today's date when I run it.

skill.title: datetime does the date maths
skill.card: The standard library already knows calendars. datetime.strptime(text, "%Y-%m-%d") turns "2026-03-01" into a date, + timedelta(days=30) moves it forward, and subtracting two dates gives a duration whose .days is a number.
skill.example:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
d = datetime.strptime("2026-01-15", "%Y-%m-%d")
due = d + timedelta(days=30)
print(due.date())
print((datetime(2026, 3, 1) - due).days)

task: Read today's date from input (YYYY-MM-DD). Each line of invoices.txt is code,issue date. An invoice is due 30 days after its issue date. For each invoice whose due date is before today, in file order, print: ~~~text F-1001: 49 days late ~~~
starter:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
today = input()
# read invoices.txt
solution:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
today = datetime.strptime(input(), "%Y-%m-%d")
with open("invoices.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        code, issued = line.strip().split(",")
        due = datetime.strptime(issued, "%Y-%m-%d") + timedelta(days=30)
        if due < today:
            print(f"{code}: {(today - due).days} days late")

title: A Ticket object for the helpdesk
brief: Our helpdesk lives in a spreadsheet and nobody knows who owns what. Before we build anything bigger I want a proper Ticket in code: a number, a title, who handles it, and whether it is closed. Closing a ticket twice should be refused.

skill.title: A class bundles data and behaviour
skill.card: class Ticket: is a blueprint. __init__ runs when you write Ticket(101, "VPN") and stores attributes on self. Methods are functions defined in the class that receive the object as self, so they can read and change its attributes.

task: Write a class Ticket(number, title): status starts at "open" and assignee at None. Methods: assign(person) sets the assignee; close() sets the status to "closed" and raises ValueError if it is already closed; label() returns #101 Printer jam on floor 2 [open]. Then read tickets.txt (lines number;title), build a list tickets of Ticket objects (number as an int) and print the label of each.
hint: In close(), test self.status first and raise ValueError("ticket already closed") before changing anything.

fs.tickets.txt:
101;Printer jam on floor 2
102;VPN keeps dropping
103;New laptop for Ines

tests.output:
#101 Printer jam on floor 2 [open]
#102 VPN keeps dropping [open]
#103 New laptop for Ines [open]

tests.name: Quiet day
tests.output: #204 Password reset [open]

test:
t = Ticket(7, "VPN down")
assert t.number == 7 and t.title == "VPN down", "number and title should be stored"
assert t.status == "open" and t.assignee is None, "a new ticket is open with assignee None"
t.assign("Sam")
assert t.assignee == "Sam", "assign('Sam') should set assignee to 'Sam'"
assert t.label() == "#7 VPN down [open]", "label() gave %r" % t.label()
t.close()
assert t.status == "closed" and t.label() == "#7 VPN down [closed]", "close() should set the status to closed"
try:
    t.close()
    raise AssertionError("closing a closed ticket should raise ValueError")
except ValueError:
    pass
assert len(tickets) == len([l for l in _fs["tickets.txt"].splitlines() if l.strip()]), "tickets should hold one Ticket per line"

title: Comments and a header
brief: The shop now writes notes in orders.txt, on lines starting with #. Your machine chokes on them. Skip those lines, and put a PICKING LIST title at the top of the sheet so the pickers grab the right paper.
task: Same as before, with two changes: lines starting with # are comments and are ignored (they are not counted either), and picking.txt starts with a line PICKING LIST before the order lines. The printed line stays Picking list: N lines, N being the order lines only.
solution:
with open("orders.txt") as f:
    lines = [line.strip() for line in f if line.strip() and not line.startswith("#")]
with open("picking.txt", "w") as out:
    out.write("PICKING LIST\n")
    for line in lines:
        sku, qty = line.split(";")
        out.write(f"[ ] {qty} x {sku}\n")
print(f"Picking list: {len(lines)} lines")
hint: Add and not line.startswith("#") to the filter, and write the title before the loop.

title: Urgent tickets and bug tickets
brief: The Ticket works. Now management wants service levels: normal tickets get an answer within 72 hours, urgent ones within 4, bug reports within 24 and they must name the broken component. I do not want three copies of the same code.

skill.title: A subclass reuses its parent
skill.card: class UrgentTicket(Ticket): gets every attribute and method of Ticket. Redefine only what differs. super().describe() calls the parent version so you can add to it, and super().__init__(...) lets the parent store its own attributes before you add yours.

task: Keep the given Ticket. Add two subclasses: - UrgentTicket(number, title): sla_hours is 4 and describe() puts URGENT in front of the parent text. - BugTicket(number, title, component): sla_hours is 24, it stores component, and describe() adds [component] after the parent text. ~~~text URGENT #31 Server room too hot: answer within 4h #32 Export button: answer within 24h [billing] ~~~
hint: Set sla_hours = 4 in the class body of UrgentTicket: the parent describe() reads self.sla_hours, so it picks up the new value.

tests.name: Service levels
tests.output:
URGENT #31 Server room too hot: answer within 4h
#32 Export button: answer within 24h [billing]

test:
assert issubclass(UrgentTicket, Ticket) and issubclass(BugTicket, Ticket), "both classes must inherit from Ticket"
assert Ticket(1, "Mouse").describe() == "#1 Mouse: answer within 72h", "do not change Ticket"
u = UrgentTicket(5, "Fire alarm")
assert u.describe() == "URGENT #5 Fire alarm: answer within 4h", "UrgentTicket(5, 'Fire alarm').describe() gave %r" % u.describe()
b = BugTicket(6, "Login fails", "auth")
assert b.number == 6 and b.title == "Login fails" and b.component == "auth", "BugTicket should store number, title and component"
assert b.describe() == "#6 Login fails: answer within 24h [auth]", "BugTicket(6, 'Login fails', 'auth').describe() gave %r" % b.describe()

title: Expense amounts that add up
brief: Our expense tool stores every amount in cents so we never get 0.1 + 0.2 surprises. I want a Money object my team can add, compare and print like a real amount. First use: the total and the biggest line of an expense report.

skill.title: Dunder methods plug into operators
skill.card: Python calls special methods for you: a + b runs a.__add__(b), a == b runs __eq__, a < b runs __lt__ (and that is enough for sorted()), and print() falls back to __repr__. sum(items, Money(0)) works once + does.

task: Write Money(cents) with + (returns a new Money), ==, < and a repr like 12.05 EUR (always 2 digits after the dot). Then read expenses.txt (lines label;cents), build the list amounts and print: ~~~text Total: 256.95 EUR Biggest: 129.00 EUR ~~~
hint: In __repr__, self.cents // 100 gives the euros and f"{self.cents % 100:02d}" the cents with a leading zero.

Biggest: 129.00 EUR

title: An audit trail for every money move
brief: The auditors want a trace of every discount and refund our scripts compute. I have a dozen of these functions and I refuse to edit each one. Can you give me a tag I just put on top of a function?

skill.title: A decorator wraps a function
skill.card: A decorator takes a function and returns a wrapper that does something extra around the real call. @audited above def refund is the same as refund = audited(refund). Use *args, **kwargs to pass every argument through, return the real result, and add @functools.wraps(func) so the function keeps its name.

task: Write a decorator audited: after each call, it appends a line name -> result to audit.log (open it with "a"), then returns the result. Keep the function name with functools.wraps. The two functions and the prints are given; with them audit.log must end up as: ~~~text apply_discount -> 60.0 refund -> -12.5 ~~~
hint: Inside wrapper: result = func(*args, **kwargs), write the line with func.__name__, then return result.
test:

assert _fs["audit.log"].splitlines() == ["apply_discount -> 60.0", "refund -> -12.5"], "audit.log contains:\n" + _fs["audit.log"]
assert apply_discount.__name__ == "apply_discount" and refund.__name__ == "refund", "use functools.wraps to keep the function names"

title: Check the order codes
brief: Our order codes look like CMD-2026-00042. Sales reps type them by hand and half the returns we get come from typos. Before the file goes to the warehouse, flag every code that does not match the format.

skill.title: re.fullmatch checks a whole format
skill.card: A regular expression describes a text pattern: \d is a digit, {4} means exactly four times, letters and - match themselves. re.fullmatch(pattern, text) returns a match only when the whole text fits, and None otherwise. Always write patterns as raw strings: r"...".

task: Each line of codes.txt is one code (strip the spaces around it). A valid code is CMD-, 4 digits, -, 5 digits. For each invalid code, in file order, print Rejected: and the code. Then print the number of valid codes: ~~~text Rejected: CMD-26-00043 Rejected: cmd-2026-00044 Valid codes: 3 ~~~
hint: The pattern is r"CMD-\d{4}-\d{5}". Use re.fullmatch, not re.search, so extra characters are refused.

title: The client ledger
brief: Big one. Every month our clients' invoices land in one text file, and it is a mess: broken invoice numbers, amounts like 'tbc'. I want a ledger with the total per client, saved to a file our other tools can reload, and a clear list of what was rejected.

skill.title: Save objects with JSON, rebuild them with a classmethod
skill.card: json.dump(data, f, indent=2) writes a dict to a file and json.load(f) reads it back. A @classmethod receives the class as cls instead of an object: Ledger.load(path) creates cls(), fills it from the file and returns it. Raising your own ValueError lets one except handle every kind of bad line.

task: Write a class Ledger with an attribute totals (a dict client to amount), add(client, amount) (adds to the client's total, rounded to 2 decimals), save(path) (JSON) and a classmethod load(path). Then read invoices.txt: lines code;client;amount. A line is rejected when the code is not INV- plus 4 digits or the amount is not a number: print Rejected: and the code. Add the good ones to a Ledger named ledger, save it to ledger.json, then print each client in alphabetical order with 2 decimals, and the number of rejected lines: ~~~text Rejected: INV-12 Rejected: INV-0006 Acme: 450.50 Belleville Bakery: 89.90 Rejected lines: 2 ~~~
